name: Repeated failed sign-ins, then a success
purpose: Find accounts that were guessed at rapidly, especially when a successful sign-in follows.
description: Counts failed authentication events per account and source address inside a short window. A success from the same account and address shortly afterwards raises severity.

attack.justification: Many failed authentications against one account from one source is the observable pattern of password guessing (Brute Force).

playbook.what: Account {username} had {observedCount} failed sign-ins from {src_ip} within {windowSeconds} seconds.
playbook.followedText: A successful sign-in for the same account and address followed, so someone got in after the failures.
playbook.why: Rapid repeated failures are how password guessing looks. A success right after means the guess may have worked, or the real user finally typed the right password.
playbook.howSure: Medium. The pattern is consistent with guessing, but a person who forgot a password or a misconfigured app can look similar. Failure count and source address are the strongest clues.
next: Ask the account owner whether they signed in from {src_ip} around this time.
Check whether {src_ip} is a known corporate, VPN or home address.
Search other sign-ins for {username} in the 24 hours around the alert (Hunt page).
Check for privilege or configuration changes by {username} after the success.
verify: The account owner confirms or denies the activity.
No further failed bursts from {src_ip} after any action taken.
If credentials were reset, the old password no longer works and new sign-ins come from expected addresses.
alternatives: A saved, outdated password in an app or script is retrying.
A vulnerability scanner or authorized test is running.
